author: sanleo
content:
> We now shape TCREATE as CREATE2
I think this might be a mistake -- including keccak(init_code) in the address calculation fucks up applications/dapps (and wallets) who might want to utilise ephemeral accounts to let users enjoy upgraded functionality as the application evolves
I get the angle of having initcode fetch runtime code (kind of like the old metamorphic contract trick, I think?), but its super complicated for app & wallet devs and requires probably a canonical implementation for the usecase I'll present

For example, lets imagine some DeFi protocol that allows you to manage lots of (possibly concentrated) liquidity positions in different protocols simultaneously, and migrate between them as APYs differ between them, rebalancing and managing these positions is common and painful, each one requires multiple txs and potentially ever evolving custom logic for every new transaction to do the rebalancing. 
What would be great then is this site lets you manage all your positions in one ephemeral account, and you select on the site (or it does it automatically) how it should be rebalanced, according to maybe new protocols or strategies that have evolved since you last rebalanced.
It then generates your initcode, does the rebalancing, etc. This code would be changing constantly, but it still needs to be at the same address each time.

Now, if we go the metamorphic route to achieve this application under the current model, the wallet has a gigantic security problem. Either it has to restrict how dApps can use ephemeral accounts in weird ways, because it would be scared of another dApp creating the same ephemeral account with new bytecode and stealing all your money, or it has to just ban them completely.

author: sanleo
content:
What I would propose instead is the hostname/site as well as perhaps some account ID is encoded into the salt or some bytes of the address calculation. The wallet then simply checks if the site you are using matches the hostname for the ephemeral account it is asking to derive, and puts up giant red warning flags or bans the tx if not.
The security model is super simple for wallets and clear for users, while still maintaining upgradeability and making the trust barrier clear.

I think also that in this system, salt alone would not be enough (since any TCREATE factory would require first 20 bytes be sender address to avoid frontrunning, and we want to allow for address space expansion as well probably, so adding extra user customisable elements (or expanding salt to say 64 bytes) would be good.)

author: gaxanh
content:
<@941650767083892737>  I'm not entirely sure what your intended design is here. That said, I've considered the address derivation several times.

Initially, I considered using only salt, but that leaves the account vulnerable to code manipulation. I then switched to sender + salt, with the idea that each account should be responsible for protecting its own target address. However, this introduces a dependency on sender, and the behavior of a ephemeral account may not necessarily be the same as that of a permanent account, so I'm not sure this is the best approach.

I then considered salt + hash(initcode), which removes the dependency on sender while still ensuring that the resulting address is associated with immutable initcode. Note that the runtime code itself is not necessarily immutable if the initcode intentionally contains logic such as if (timestamp > X) deploy A else B. However, for compatibility with CREATE2, I eventually decided to keep sender + salt + hash(initcode).

Regarding metamorphic contracts, if you're referring to the CREATE3 model, then essentially TCREATE is just replacing the TCREATE/CREATE path while making it cheaper.

If instead you mean that a ephemeral account could have different code on each transaction/session, then the code-manipulation issue mentioned above still applies. However, if the intention is to use initcode as part of more advanced DeFi strategies, that initcode would need to be bound to the user's signed data. Adding a guarantee that the ephemeral address is tied to the user's account would be sufficient, which effectively brings us back to the sender || salt approach I mentioned above.

Also, the EVM already has EVM interpreter contracts, for example [Analog Labs' EVM interpreter](https://github.com/Analog-Labs/evm-interpreter)
. If your goal is simply to delegate assets to someone while enforcing/attesting to changes in behavior, an interpreter-based approach may already fit that use case.
